intro: To run UI tests in Xcode on Mac, you use the XCTest framework to interact with your application interface. You can trigger these tests using the Test Navigator, keyboard shortcuts, or by clicking the diamond icons in your source code.
tldr: Add a UI Testing Bundle target via File > New > Target.
Use ⌘ + U to run all tests in your scheme.
Open the Test Navigator with ⌘ + 6 to run specific tests.

blocks.text: Setting up your UI testing environment

Before you can run tests, you need a UI Testing Bundle target in your project. This target contains the code that drives your app during the test process. If you do not have one, go to File > New > Target. Type Test into the search bar and select UI Testing Bundle. Click Next, provide a name like MyAppUITests, and click Finish. This adds a new folder to your project navigator.
How to run UI tests using the Test Navigator

The Test Navigator is the central hub for managing your testing suite. Press ⌘ + 6 to bring it into view. You will see a list of your test bundles, classes, and individual methods. Hover over any item in the list to reveal a diamond-shaped run button. Clicking this button executes that specific test or group of tests. It is a clean way to isolate a single feature without running your entire suite.
Generating test code with the recorder

Writing UI test code from scratch is tedious. Xcode includes a recorder to help you generate the necessary Swift code. Open your UI test file and place your cursor inside a test function. Look at the bottom of the editor window for the red record button. When you click it, Xcode launches your app in the Simulator. Every interaction you perform in the app is converted into code in your editor. Once you finish your sequence, click the record button again to stop. Review the generated code to ensure it captured the elements you intended to test.

blocks.text: Best practices for UI testing in Xcode

Always prioritize accessibility identifiers. Your test code relies on these to find elements reliably. Avoid relying on hardcoded coordinates or visual positions. If a button moves, your test might fail if it looks for a specific screen location. Keep your test code modular. Create helper methods for common sequences like logging in or navigating to a specific screen. This makes your test suite easier to maintain as your app grows.

faq.question: Can I use Swift Testing for UI tests?
faq.answer: No. As of current Xcode versions, Swift Testing is not supported for UI tests. You must use the XCTest framework for all UI testing tasks.

faq.question: Why are my tests failing to find UI elements?
faq.answer: This is often due to missing accessibility identifiers. Check that your UI elements have unique accessibility identifiers set in your code or in the Attributes Inspector.

faq.question: What is the keyboard shortcut to run tests?
faq.answer: The primary shortcut to run all tests in your current scheme is ⌘ + U.

steps.name: Run the tests
steps.text: Press ⌘ + U to execute all tests or click the diamond icon in the editor gutter to run a specific one.
